chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: The chapter follows the book's own order: ten thousand and the new TTh column first, then reading, writing, patterns, comparing and ordering, the number line and rounding, and finally the journeys and puzzles that use large numbers. Every idea starts with something the student does, and the tools put number cards, tokens and number lines in the student's hands.

points.title: Build it, then name it
points.text: Students first build a number from tokens or cards and only then read it, write it in digits with commas and write its name. The chart shows where every digit sits.

points.title: Predict before the reveal
points.text: Each idea opens with a question answered before the picture: what comes after nine thousand, which of two numbers is greater, which ten is nearest to 2,346.

points.title: Tools only where handling is the idea
points.text: Ten tools, each used once: an odometer, ten-thousand builder, token table, pattern rule finder, compare chart, number line, rabbit rounder, vehicle loader, digit difference machine and the king's stable. Ideas about meaning and puzzles that need only a discussion carry no tool.

points.title: Every book question has its own video
points.text: Each Let Us Do, Let Us Think and puzzle question is its own short video, in a Questions topic that follows the idea it practises.

modules.module_name: Big Numbers: Reading, Writing and Comparing
modules.module_summary: Counting thousands up to ten thousand, the new Ten Thousands column, reading and writing five-digit numbers with commas and number names, patterns in sequences, comparing and ordering large numbers, placing them on a number line, swapping digits, expanded form and counting in tens, hundreds and thousands.

concepts.concept_name: How far did you go on your last trip?

content.text:
When was the last time you went on a long trip? Where did you go? How did you travel? What was the duration of your trip? How much distance did you cover? Ask the elders who went with you to help you answer these questions.
Human beings have always been interested in travelling. About a hundred years ago, there were far fewer vehicles than today. There were animal-drawn carts, cars, and trains. Long before this, thousands of years ago, people travelled long distances on foot or used animals to travel from one place to another. They also built boats and ships to travel across lakes, rivers, and seas. Boats were probably the first form of transport invented by humans, much before bullock carts! Do you know how many vehicles are currently there in your state?

concepts.concept_name: Try it: read the odometer

content.text:
An odometer shows how many kilometres a vehicle has covered.
Each wheel of the odometer is one place: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands and now ten thousands.
When the ones wheel passes 9 it turns back to 0 and moves the next wheel by one.

concepts.concept_name: What comes after nine thousand?

content.text:
How do you write numbers to show several thousand objects?
Let us start with 1,000. What numbers do we get when we keep adding a thousand?
1,000 2,000 ... 9,000
What number do we get when we add a thousand to 9,000? We get ten thousand. How do we write this number?

Let us start with 1,000. What numbers do we get when we keep adding a thousand?
What number do we get when we add a thousand to 9,000? We get ten thousand. How do we write this number?

content.text:
1. Predict first: if you keep adding a thousand to 1,000, which number comes after 9,000?
2. 1,000, 2,000, 3,000, and so on up to 9,000. Each step adds one more thousand.
3. 9,000 + 1,000 = 10,000. Ten thousands make ten thousand, and the number needs a new place.

content.text:
Worked example: Keep adding a thousand to 1,000. Which number do you reach after 9,000, and how many thousands is it?
1. 1,000, 2,000, 3,000, 4,000, 5,000, 6,000, 7,000, 8,000, 9,000.
2. One more thousand: 9,000 + 1,000 = 10,000.
3. 10,000 is 10 thousands, called ten thousand.
Answer: 10,000, which is ten thousand and is 10 thousands

concepts.concept_name: The new TTh column

content.text:
Look at the table below and notice the pattern of writing numbers. In the place value chart, we have added another column, TTh. It stands for ten thousand.
10 Ones = 1 Ten = 10, 10 Tens = 1 Hundred = 100, 10 Hundreds = 1 Thousand = 1,000.
In the same way, 10 Thousands = Ten Thousand = 10,000.
We use a comma to help us read large numbers easily.

content.text:
1. Predict first: the chart has columns for ones, tens, hundreds and thousands. Where will 10 thousands go?
2. Ten of one place always make one of the next place to the left: 10 ones, 10 tens, 10 hundreds, 10 thousands.
3. So 10 thousands make 1 in a new column, TTh, with zeros in the four places to its right: 10,000.
4. The comma sits after the thousands place and helps the eye read the number.

concepts.concept_name: Reading numbers in the Indian place value system

content.text:
Do you remember how we read and write numbers in the Indian place value system? We use the same ten digits 0 to 9 in different places to write larger numbers.
For example, 1,380 = 1 Thousand + 3 Hundreds + 8 Tens + 0 Ones.
9,123 = 9 Thousands + 1 Hundred + 2 Tens + 3 Ones.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students count in thousands up to 9,000 and say that adding one more thousand gives ten thousand.
Students extend the place value chart with a TTh column, state that 10 thousands is 1 ten thousand and that 10 tens, 10 hundreds and 10 thousands each make the next place, and write 10,000.
Students read and write a number as thousands, hundreds, tens and ones, such as 1,380 and 9,123, using the same ten digits in different places.
Students build numbers from ones to ten thousand by dropping tokens in the place value chart, watch ten tokens regroup into one of the next place, and read each number aloud.

concepts.concept_name: Numbers just after ten thousand

content.text:
Let us see how we write numbers beyond 10,000 and how we name them. We write them in the same way as numbers below 9,999. You can use the tokens given in the end of the book.
10,001: TTh 1, Th 0, H 0, T 0, O 1: Ten thousand one.
10,002: TTh 1, Th 0, H 0, T 0, O 2: Ten thousand two.
10,010: TTh 1, Th 0, H 0, T 1, O 0: Ten thousand ten.
10,024: TTh 1, Th 0, H 0, T 2, O 4: Ten thousand twenty-four.

content.text:
1. Predict first: one 10,000 token and one 1 token, what number is it and how do we say it?
2. 10,000 + 1 = 10,001, said ten thousand one. The zeros hold the Th, H and T places.
3. The same idea works for 10,002, 10,010 and 10,024: the TTh digit stays 1 and only the small places change.

Worked example: One 10,000 token with two 1 tokens, one 10,000 token with one 10 token, and one 10,000 token with two 10 tokens and four 1 tokens. Write each number and its name.
1. 10,000 + 2 = 10,002, Ten thousand two.
2. 10,000 + 10 = 10,010, Ten thousand ten.
3. 10,000 + 20 + 4 = 10,024, Ten thousand twenty-four.
Answer: 10,002 is ten thousand two, 10,010 is ten thousand ten and 10,024 is ten thousand twenty-four

tool_config.design_brief: Class 5 tool brief: interactive and doer-based, the student performs actions and does not only watch. The student can build and rearrange numbers, compare values, place markers on number lines, complete patterns and solve problems. Colourful, clear and engaging: number cards, place value tokens, number lines, arrows, visual counters and real-life travel illustrations, all of which can be selected, moved, changed or arranged. A simple uncluttered layout with one prominent main visual and only the controls that are needed. Immediate visual feedback: numbers update, markers move and correct arrangements are highlighted. Hints and feedback help the student discover the answer and never reveal it. Hands-on, visually engaging and conceptually clear.

Students count the tokens of each kind to write a number such as 10,033, 10,458, 11,214 or 13,520, fill its TTh, Th, H, T, O digits and say its name.
Students write 13,520, 20,000 and 45,867 as numbers and in words and see that the thousands part is read first.
Students build five-digit numbers from tokens, write each number with commas in the TTh to O chart, and write the number name from the thousands part first.

concepts.concept_name: Adding the same number each time

content.text:
1. Predict first: 2,000, 2,500, 3,000. What do you add to get from one number to the next?
2. Subtract each number from the one after it: 2,500 − 2,000 = 500 and 3,000 − 2,500 = 500.
3. The change is the same each time, 500, so the rule is add 500. The next numbers are 3,500, 4,000 and 4,500.
content.publication_text:
1. Predict first: 2,000, 2,500, 3,000. What do you add to get from one number to the next?
2. Subtract each number from the one after it: 2,500 − 2,000 = 500 and 3,000 − 2,500 = 500.
3. The change is the same each time, 500, so the rule is add 500. The next numbers are 3,500, 4,000 and 4,500.

content.text:

tool_config.title: Pattern Rule Finder: What Is the Jump?
tool_config.idea: A pattern of numbers has a rule. Jumping from one number to the next on a number line shows how much is added or taken away each time, and the same jump gives the next numbers.
tool_config.screen: A row of number cards with blanks, a number line that shows an arrow for each jump, a jump-size dial, and a Test the rule button that fills the blanks with the chosen jump.
student_does: Look at two neighbouring cards and drag the dial to the jump between them.
Press Test the rule and watch the arrow jumps fill the blanks.
Check that every card in the row now follows the rule.
Change the rule and see which cards no longer fit.
challenges: Sequence 456, 567, 678: find the jump and fill four blanks.
Sequence 1,050, blank, 3,150, 4,200: find the jump and the missing card.
Sequence 5,501, 6,401, 7,301: find the jump and fill two blanks.
Sequence 10,100, 10,200, 10,300 continuing to 10,900.
Sequence 10,992, 10,993: find the jump.
Sequence 73,005, 72,004: is the rule add or subtract, and how much?
feedback: Each correct jump draws an arrow in the colour of its rule; a wrong jump shows the two cards that do not match.
A blank filled by the rule turns green and keeps the arrow behind it.
A rule that adds when the cards fall is shown as an arrow pointing the wrong way.
tool_config.done_when: Every sequence is completed and the rule is named in words.

hint_ladder.text: How far apart are the first two cards?
Is the next card bigger or smaller than the one before?
Subtract the smaller neighbouring card from the bigger and try that jump on the next pair.
The jump between the first two cards is shown; test it on the third and fourth cards.

tool_config.design_brief: Class 5 tool brief: interactive and doer-based, the student performs actions and does not only watch. The student can build and rearrange numbers, compare values, place markers on number lines, complete patterns and solve problems. Colourful, clear and engaging: number cards, place value tokens, number lines, arrows, visual counters and real-life travel illustrations, all of which can be selected, moved, changed or arranged. A simple uncluttered layout with one prominent main visual and only the controls that are needed. Immediate visual feedback: numbers update, markers move and correct arrangements are highlighted. Hints and feedback help the student discover the answer and never reveal it. Hands-on, visually engaging and conceptually clear.

media.title: Can a row of numbers grow by just one, or by twenty, each time?
media.context: We the Travellers - I. Question video: one question from the book. It opens only after the student has tried the question, and it hints before it tells. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Kavya's father sells bus tickets in Chennai and finds rows of serial numbers with some missing. The video finds the rule of four rows, small ones too.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: the rule can be small, and the whole gap must be used. Watch for children who read one digit of the gap, like the tens digit.

concepts.concept_name: More digits, greater number

content.text:
1. Predict first: which is greater, 9,876 or 10,012?
2. Count the digits first. 9,876 has four digits and 10,012 has five digits.
3. A number with more digits is greater, because its leftmost digit sits in a bigger place. The size of the first digit does not matter when the digits are not equal in number.

content.text:
Worked example: Which is greater, 9,876 or 10,012?
1. 9,876 has 4 digits and 10,012 has 5 digits.
2. The number with more digits is greater.
3. 10,012 is greater, even though 9 is greater than 1.
Answer: 10,012 is greater than 9,876

concepts.concept_name: Same number of digits: compare from the left

content.text:
1. Predict first: 56,321 and 56,298 both have five digits. Which is greater, and which digit tells you?
2. Put both numbers on the place value chart, TTh Th H T O, one below the other.
3. Move from the left. TTh is 5 and 5, equal. Th is 6 and 6, equal. H is 3 and 2, different, so stop.
4. The number with the bigger digit at the first place where the digits differ is greater.

concepts.concept_name: Arranging numbers in order

content.text:
1. Predict first: to arrange 3,450, 34,500, 345 and 4,035 in increasing order, which one comes first?
2. Group by number of digits, then compare inside each group from the left.
3. Increasing means smaller to greater, ascending. Decreasing means greater to smaller, descending.
4. A number line also arranges numbers: the greater a number, the farther to the right.

content.text:
Let Us Do 3, arrange in increasing order: Arrange in increasing order: 40,347, 34,407, 40,473, 34,740, 73,404, 74,430, 47,340 and 18,926.
1. 18,926 is the only number with TTh digit 1.
2. With TTh digit 3: 34,407 and 34,740. Th is 4 and 4; H is 4 and 7, so 34,407 is less than 34,740.
3. With TTh digit 4: 40,347, 40,473 and 47,340. Th is 0, 0 and 7, so 47,340 is last of the three. H is 3 and 4, so 40,347 is less than 40,473.
4. With TTh digit 7: 73,404 and 74,430. Th is 3 and 4, so 73,404 is less than 74,430.
Answer: 18,926, 34,407, 34,740, 40,347, 40,473, 47,340, 73,404, 74,430

content.text:
Let Us Do 4, the student's claim: A student said 9,990 is greater than 49,014 because 9 is greater than 4. Is the student correct? Why or why not?
1. 9,990 has 4 digits and 49,014 has 5 digits.
2. A number with more digits is greater, so 49,014 is greater.
3. The student compared 9 with 4 as if both numbers had the same number of digits.
Answer: The student is not correct: 9,990 < 49,014, because 49,014 has more digits

content.text:
Let Us Do (second set) 3, the two cars: Ravi's car has been driven for 56,987 km till now. Sheetal's car has been driven 67,543 km. Whose car has been driven more?
1. Both numbers have 5 digits, so compare from the left.
2. TTh: 5 and 6, and 6 is greater than 5.
3. So 67,543 is greater than 56,987.
Answer: Sheetal's car, 67,543 km, has been driven more

content.text:
Let Us Do (second set) 4, prices of electric bikes: Arrange the prices in ascending (increasing) order: 90,000, 89,999, 94,983, 49,900, 93,743 and 39,999.
1. TTh digits: 9, 8, 9, 4, 9 and 3. The smallest is 39,999 (TTh 3), then 49,900 (TTh 4), then 89,999 (TTh 8).
2. The three numbers starting with 9: 90,000, 94,983 and 93,743. Th is 0, 4 and 3.
3. So 90,000 is less than 93,743, which is less than 94,983.
Answer: 39,999, 49,900, 89,999, 90,000, 93,743, 94,983

Let Us Do (second set) 4, prices of electric bikes: Arrange the prices in ascending (increasing) order: 90,000, 89,999, 94,983, 49,900, 93,743 and 39,999.
1. TTh digits: 9, 8, 9, 4, 9 and 3. The smallest is 39,999 (TTh 3), then 49,900 (TTh 4), then 89,999 (TTh 8).
2. The three numbers starting with 9: 90,000, 94,983 and 93,743. Th is 0, 4 and 3.
3. So 90,000 is less than 93,743, which is less than 94,983.
Answer: 39,999, 49,900, 89,999, 90,000, 93,743, 94,983
content.question: Arrange the prices in ascending (increasing) order: 90,000, 89,999, 94,983, 49,900, 93,743 and 39,999.
steps: TTh digits: 9, 8, 9, 4, 9 and 3. The smallest is 39,999 (TTh 3), then 49,900 (TTh 4), then 89,999 (TTh 8).
The three numbers starting with 9: 90,000, 94,983 and 93,743. Th is 0, 4 and 3.
So 90,000 is less than 93,743, which is less than 94,983.

content.text:
Let Us Do (second set) 5, population of towns: Arrange the populations in descending (decreasing) order: Town 1 65,232, Town 2 53,231, Town 3 56,380, Town 4 51,336, Town 5 45,858 and Town 6 66,540.
1. All have 5 digits. TTh is 6, 5, 5, 5, 4 and 6.
2. TTh 6: Town 6 (66,540) and Town 1 (65,232). Th is 6 and 5, so Town 6 is greater.
3. TTh 5: Town 3 (56,380), Town 2 (53,231) and Town 4 (51,336). Th is 6, 3 and 1.
4. Town 5 (45,858) has TTh 4, the smallest.
Answer: Town 6 (66,540), Town 1 (65,232), Town 3 (56,380), Town 2 (53,231), Town 4 (51,336), Town 5 (45,858)

hint_ladder.text: How many digits does each number have?
If both have the same digits, which is the first place where they differ?
Compare the leftmost digits that differ; the bigger digit there gives the bigger number.
For 9,990 and 49,014: 49,014 has five digits and 9,990 has four, so 49,014 is greater.

tool_config.design_brief: Class 5 tool brief: interactive and doer-based, the student performs actions and does not only watch. The student can build and rearrange numbers, compare values, place markers on number lines, complete patterns and solve problems. Colourful, clear and engaging: number cards, place value tokens, number lines, arrows, visual counters and real-life travel illustrations, all of which can be selected, moved, changed or arranged. A simple uncluttered layout with one prominent main visual and only the controls that are needed. Immediate visual feedback: numbers update, markers move and correct arrangements are highlighted. Hints and feedback help the student discover the answer and never reveal it. Hands-on, visually engaging and conceptually clear.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students compare numbers with a different number of digits and say that the number with more digits is greater, whatever its first digit.
Students compare numbers with the same number of digits by looking at each place from the left on the place value chart, and stop at the first place where the digits differ.
Students arrange numbers in increasing (ascending) and decreasing (descending) order by sorting them by number of digits first and then comparing within each group.
Students compare and order numbers on the compare chart, with the digits in a place value chart and the numbers as markers on a number line.

concepts.concept_name: Where does a number sit on the line?

content.text:
1. Predict first: on a line marked 0, 20,000, 40,000, 60,000 and 80,000, where will 47,340 sit?
2. Find the two marks it lies between. 47,340 is more than 40,000 and less than 60,000.
3. Then look at how far it is from the nearer mark. It is only 7,340 past 40,000, so it sits closer to 40,000.
4. The greater the number, the farther to the right it is.

content.text:
Worked example: Between which two marks of 0, 20,000, 40,000, 60,000 and 80,000 does 47,340 sit, and which mark is it nearer to?
1. 47,340 is more than 40,000 and less than 60,000.
2. 47,340 − 40,000 = 7,340 and 60,000 − 47,340 = 12,660.
3. 7,340 is smaller than 12,660, so it is nearer to 40,000.
Answer: 47,340 sits between 40,000 and 60,000, nearer to 40,000

concepts.concept_name: Numbers between two numbers

content.text:
1. Predict first: name a number between 12,350 and 12,800. Is it the only one?
2. A number between them has to be greater than the first and less than the second. Keep the first digits the same and change the hundreds.
3. There are many such numbers. We can name some in steps of 100: 12,400, 12,500, 12,600 and 12,700.

concepts.concept_name: Digit swap

content.text:
1. Predict first: in 2,935, which two digits do you swap to get the largest number?
2. Swapping two digits changes two places at once. The place on the left matters more.
3. To make a number large, put the biggest digit in the leftmost place. To make it small, put the smallest digit there, if you can.

content.text:
Worked example: Swap two digits of 2,935 to make the largest number and the smallest number you can.
1. Largest: the biggest digit, 9, should be in the thousands place. Swap 2 and 9 to get 9,235.
2. Smallest: 2 is already the smallest digit, in the thousands place. Now put the next smallest, 3, in the hundreds place: swap 9 and 3 to get 2,395.
Answer: Largest 9,235 (swap 2 and 9), smallest 2,395 (swap 9 and 3)

tool_config.title: Number Line Placer: Where Does It Go?
tool_config.idea: A number line shows how far a number is from 0. Marking a number between two benchmark numbers by reading its place values tells us where on the line it sits.
tool_config.screen: A long number line with benchmark ticks at 0, 20,000, 40,000, 60,000 and 80,000, number cards to drag onto the line, a zoom bar that shows the line between two ticks in finer steps, and a ruler of place values under the chosen number.
student_does: Drag a number card to the place on the line where you think it belongs.
Zoom into the part of the line between two ticks to place it more exactly.
Press Check to see the number's true position and how far off the marker was.
Move the marker again until it sits on the number.
challenges: Place 40,347 and 40,473: which is to the right?
Place 34,407 and 34,740 between 20,000 and 40,000.
Place 73,404 and 74,430 between 60,000 and 80,000.
Place 47,340 and 18,926 and say which tick each is nearest to.
Place all eight numbers and read them from left to right.
Find a number between 23,568 and 24,234 and place it.
feedback: A correctly placed marker locks in with a tick mark and the number printed above.
A marker placed too far shows an arrow back towards the true place, never the exact spot.
When the line is zoomed, the ticks update to the new step and the cards already on the line stay.
tool_config.done_when: Every card is done with all markers on their true places.

hint_ladder.text: Between which two ticks does the number sit?
Look at the thousands and ten thousands digits to decide which two ticks.
Zoom into the stretch between those ticks and use the hundreds digit to place it.
Between 40,000 and 60,000, the number 47,340 sits just over a third of the way along.

tool_config.design_brief: Class 5 tool brief: interactive and doer-based, the student performs actions and does not only watch. The student can build and rearrange numbers, compare values, place markers on number lines, complete patterns and solve problems. Colourful, clear and engaging: number cards, place value tokens, number lines, arrows, visual counters and real-life travel illustrations, all of which can be selected, moved, changed or arranged. A simple uncluttered layout with one prominent main visual and only the controls that are needed. Immediate visual feedback: numbers update, markers move and correct arrangements are highlighted. Hints and feedback help the student discover the answer and never reveal it. Hands-on, visually engaging and conceptually clear.

media.title: How do you swap digits to land in a range?
media.context: We the Travellers - I. Question video: one question from the book. It opens only after the student has tried the question, and it hints before it tells. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.

concepts.concept_name: Expanded form

content.text:
1. Predict first: what does 6,508 add up from?
2. Each digit has a value: 6 in the thousands is 6,000, 5 in the hundreds is 500, 0 in the tens is 0, 8 in the ones is 8.
3. Write the values with plus signs. A zero digit adds nothing, so its place can be left out of the sum, but the zero still holds the place in the number.

concepts.concept_name: Counting in tens, hundreds and thousands

content.text:
1. Predict first: 983 is 98 tens and 3 ones. Can you also write it as 90 tens and some ones?
2. 90 tens is 900. The remaining 83 are ones: 983 = 90 Tens + 83 Ones.
3. The number is the same; only the way of grouping changes. Both are correct.

content.text:
Worked example: Write 983 as 90 Tens + __ Ones, and 4,560 as 45 Hundreds + __ Ones.
1. 90 Tens = 900, and 983 − 900 = 83, so 983 = 90 Tens + 83 Ones.
2. 45 Hundreds = 4,500, and 4,560 − 4,500 = 60, so 4,560 = 45 Hundreds + 60 Ones.
Answer: 983 = 90 Tens + 83 Ones and 4,560 = 45 Hundreds + 60 Ones

concepts.concept_name: How many notes?

content.text:
1. Predict first: how many 10 rupee notes make 3,250 rupees?
2. 3 Tens is 30, 90 Tens is 900 and 700 Tens is 7,000. In 3,250, the number of tens is 325.
3. For hundreds, drop the last two digits: 32 hundreds are in 3,250. For thousands drop the last three: 3 thousands.
4. For 500 notes, count how many hundreds there are and divide by 5; the leftover is not enough for another note.

content.text:
Worked example: How many notes of 10, of 100, of 1,000 and of 500 are there in 3,250?
1. Notes of 10: 3,250 has 325 tens.
2. Notes of 100: 3,250 has 32 hundreds, with 50 left.
3. Notes of 1,000: 3,250 has 3 thousands, with 250 left.
4. Notes of 500: 32 hundreds is 5 hundreds six times with 2 hundreds over, so 6 notes of 500.
Answer: 325 notes of 10, 32 notes of 100, 3 notes of 1,000 and 6 notes of 500

content.text:
Let Us Do (second set) 8 (d) to (g), more place value forms: Fill in the blanks: (d) 5,621 = 4 Thousand + __ Hundreds + 2 Tens + __ Ones (e) 7,069 = __ Thousand + 20 Hundreds + __ Ones (f) 37,608 = __ Ten Thousand + 17 Thousand + __ Hundreds + 8 Ones (g) 43,001 = 3 Ten Thousand + __ Thousand + __ Hundreds + 1 Ones.
1. (d) 5,621 − 4,000 = 1,621. 2 Tens and 1 One use 21, so the Hundreds are 1,600, which is 16 Hundreds, and the Ones are 1.
2. (e) 20 Hundreds is 2,000, so the Thousand part is 5,000 and 7,069 − 7,000 = 69 Ones.
3. (f) 17 Thousand is 17,000 and 8 Ones is 8. 37,608 − 17,000 − 8 = 20,600, so 2 Ten Thousand and 6 Hundreds.
4. (g) 3 Ten Thousand is 30,000 and 1 One is 1. 43,001 − 30,000 − 1 = 13,000, so 13 Thousand and 0 Hundreds.
Answer: (d) 16 Hundreds and 1 Ones; (e) 5 Thousand and 69 Ones; (f) 2 Ten Thousand and 6 Hundreds; (g) 13 Thousand and 0 Hundreds

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students write a number as the sum of the value of its digits, and use zero to hold an empty place.
Students write a number as tens plus ones, hundreds plus ones, and thousands plus hundreds plus tens plus ones, and see that there is more than one way.
Students tell how many notes of 10, 100, 500 or 1,000 make up a number by dividing the number into groups, and see that the leftover amount is not a full note.
Students write expanded forms and counts of tens, hundreds, thousands and notes for the numbers in the book's exercises.

concepts.concept_name: The nearest ten

content.text:
1. Predict first: a rabbit sits at 2,346. Its food is at the two neighbouring tens. Which one is nearer?
2. The neighbouring tens of 2,346 are 2,340 and 2,350.
3. To 2,350 it needs 4 jumps and to 2,340 it needs 6 jumps. The fewest jumps wins.
4. 2,350 is the nearest ten of 2,346.

content.text:
Worked example: The rabbit is at 2,346 and its food is at 2,340 and 2,350. Which is the nearest ten?
1. 2,350 − 2,346 = 4 jumps to 2,350.
2. 2,346 − 2,340 = 6 jumps to 2,340.
3. 4 is less than 6, so the rabbit goes to 2,350.
Answer: 2,350 is the nearest ten of 2,346, with 4 jumps

concepts.concept_name: The nearest thousand and the halfway rule

content.text:
1. Predict first: the same rabbit again, food at the two neighbouring thousands, 2,000 and 3,000.
2. To 2,000 it needs 346 jumps and to 3,000 it needs 654 jumps, so 2,000 is the nearest thousand.
3. Look at the middle of 2,000 and 3,000: it is 2,500. A number exactly in the middle is the same distance from both. By the usual rule, it goes to the bigger one, 3,000.

tool_config.design_brief: Class 5 tool brief: interactive and doer-based, the student performs actions and does not only watch. The student can build and rearrange numbers, compare values, place markers on number lines, complete patterns and solve problems. Colourful, clear and engaging: number cards, place value tokens, number lines, arrows, visual counters and real-life travel illustrations, all of which can be selected, moved, changed or arranged. A simple uncluttered layout with one prominent main visual and only the controls that are needed. Immediate visual feedback: numbers update, markers move and correct arrangements are highlighted. concepts.concept_name: How people travelled then and now

content.text:
1. Predict first: which animal would you use to travel in a desert, and which in a snow-covered hill?
2. In the past people travelled on foot, on animals and in boats and sailing ships. Bullocks, horses, donkeys, mules and elephants carried people; yaks, dogs and reindeer were used in hilly and snow-covered regions, and camels in deserts.
3. Now people use bicycles, motorbikes, cars, buses, trains, ships and aeroplanes. Submarines go deep under water and spacecraft go to outer space.

content.text:
Worked example: Which would be used to travel (a) in a desert, (b) in a snow-covered region, (c) deep under water, (d) to outer space?
1. (a) Camels have been used in deserts.
2. (b) Yaks, dogs and reindeer have been used in hilly and snow-covered regions.
3. (c) Submarines are used to go deep under water.
4. (d) Humans use spacecraft to travel to outer space.
Answer: (a) camel, (b) yak, dog or reindeer, (c) submarine, (d) spacecraft

concepts.concept_name: How far in one hour?

content.text:
1. Predict first: in one hour, how far can a person go on foot, and how far in a spacecraft?
2. In an hour a person can generally travel 3 to 5 km on foot, 10 to 15 km on horseback and 12 to 20 km by cycle.
3. By motorbike 40 to 60 km, by train 40 to 160 km, by ship 25 to 45 km and by aircraft 750 to 920 km.
4. A spacecraft covers a minimum of 28,000 km in an hour. The distances range from a 1-digit number to a 5-digit number.

concepts.concept_name: Distance in many hours

content.text:
1. Predict first: a motorbike goes 50 km in one hour. How far in 3 hours at the same speed?
2. In 1 hour 50 km, in 2 hours 50 + 50 = 100 km, in 3 hours 150 km.
3. The distance in many hours is the distance in one hour times the number of hours.

content.text:
Worked example: A motorbike covers 50 km in one hour. How far does it go in 3 hours at the same speed?
1. 1 hour: 50 km. 2 hours: 50 + 50 = 100 km.
2. 3 hours: 100 + 50 = 150 km.
3. Or 50 × 3 = 150 km.
Answer: 150 km

content.text:
Let Us Do 2, vehicles (a) to (d): A school has 461 girls and 439 boys. How many vehicles are needed for all of them to go on a trip using (a) bicycle (2) (b) autorickshaw (3) (c) car (4) (d) big car (6)?
1. Total students: 461 + 439 = 900.
2. (a) 900 ÷ 2 = 450 bicycles.
3. (b) 900 ÷ 3 = 300 autorickshaws.
4. (c) 900 ÷ 4 = 225 cars.
5. (d) 900 ÷ 6 = 150 big cars.
Answer: (a) 450 (b) 300 (c) 225 (d) 150

2. (e) 900 ÷ 10 = 90 tempo travellers.
3. (f) 900 ÷ 20 = 45 boats.
4. (g) 900 ÷ 25 = 36 minibuses.
5. (h) 900 ÷ 180 = 5 aeroplanes.
Answer: (e) 90 (f) 45 (g) 36 (h) 5

content.text:
Let Us Do 1, the cyclist: A cyclist can cover 15 km in one hour. How much distance will she cover in 4 hours, if she maintains the same speed?
1. 1 hour: 15 km. 2 hours: 15 + 15 = 30 km.
2. 3 hours: 30 + 15 = 45 km. 4 hours: 45 + 15 = 60 km.
3. Or 15 × 4 = 60.
Answer: 60 km

tool_config.idea: To carry a group of people, divide the number of people by the number each vehicle carries. When there is a remainder, one more vehicle is needed for the people left over.
tool_config.screen: A crowd of 900 people shown in groups of 10, a row of eight vehicles (bicycle 2, autorickshaw 3, car 4, big car 6, tempo traveller 10, boat 20, minibus 25, aeroplane 180), a Load button that fills a chosen vehicle with people and a counter of vehicles used.

900 people with tempo travellers, boats and minibuses.

feedback: Each loaded vehicle drops one token on a tally and the people left count down.

hint_ladder.text: How many people can one vehicle carry?
How many times can that number be taken out of 900 before nobody is left?
Divide 900 by the number each vehicle carries; if some people are left, one more vehicle is needed.

tool_config.design_brief: Class 5 tool brief: interactive and doer-based, the student performs actions and does not only watch. The student can build and rearrange numbers, compare values, place markers on number lines, complete patterns and solve problems. Colourful, clear and engaging: number cards, place value tokens, number lines, arrows, visual counters and real-life travel illustrations, all of which can be selected, moved, changed or arranged. A simple uncluttered layout with one prominent main visual and only the controls that are needed. Immediate visual feedback: numbers update, markers move and correct arrangements are highlighted. Hints and feedback help the student discover the answer and never reveal it. Hands-on, visually engaging and conceptually clear.

concepts.concept_name: How many words in a book?

content.text:
We saw that the distance (in kilometre) covered by different means of transport in an hour can range from a 1-digit number to a 5-digit number. Can we find other contexts around us that contain numbers in this range?
A book has around 200 pages, and each page has about 50 words. The book therefore has about 10,000 words in all.
Find something in the textbook whose count is a 4-digit number.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a book has about 200 pages and about 50 words on each page. About how many words is that?
2. 50 words on 1 page, 100 on 2 pages, 500 on 10 pages, 5,000 on 100 pages, so 10,000 on 200 pages.
3. 200 × 50 = 10,000. When we count a small part and multiply, we do not need to count every word.

content.text:
Worked example: A book has around 200 pages and each page has about 50 words. About how many words are in the book?
1. 100 pages have 100 × 50 = 5,000 words.
2. 200 pages are 2 times as many: 5,000 × 2 = 10,000 words.
3. 10,000 is a 5-digit number.
Answer: About 10,000 words, a 5-digit number

concepts.concept_name: The river crossing

content.text:
Sanju and Mira are traveling on a train. To pass time, they challenge each other with games and puzzles.
Mira poses the river crossing puzzle to Sanju. A boatman wants to cross a river in a boat. He has to take a lion, a sheep, and a bundle of grass with him. He can take one of them at a time. If the sheep and grass are left on the shore, the sheep will eat the grass. And, if the sheep and lion are left on the shore, the lion will eat the sheep.
How can the boatman take the lion, sheep, and grass across the river? Help him so that he can ferry the lion, sheep, and grass across the river safely, and in the minimum number of trips.

Mira poses the river crossing puzzle to Sanju. A boatman wants to cross a river in a boat. He has to take a lion, a sheep, and a bundle of grass with him. He can take one of them at a time. If the sheep and grass are left on the shore, the sheep will eat the grass. And, if the sheep and lion are left on the shore, the lion will eat the sheep.
How can the boatman take the lion, sheep, and grass across the river? Help him so that he can ferry the lion, sheep, and grass across the river safely, and in the minimum number of trips.

content.text:
1. Predict first: which of the three should the boatman take first, so that nothing is eaten?
2. The sheep is the problem: it cannot be left with the grass, and it cannot be left with the lion.
3. Take the sheep first. The lion and the grass can be left together, because the lion does not eat grass.
4. Then bring something back so that the sheep is never alone with the lion or the grass.

content.text:
Worked example: How can the boatman take the lion, the sheep and the grass across the river safely in the fewest trips?
1. Trip 1: take the sheep across. The lion and the grass are safe together on the first shore.
2. Trip 2: come back alone. Trip 3: take the lion across. The lion and the sheep cannot be left together when the boatman leaves.
3. Trip 4: bring the sheep back. Trip 5: take the grass across. The lion and the grass are safe together on the far shore.
4. Trip 6: come back alone. Trip 7: take the sheep across.

concepts.concept_name: The pile of pebbles

content.text:
Sanju introduces a game called pile of pebbles to Mira.
There are two piles of pebbles. Each pile contains 7 pebbles. Each player can pick as many pebbles they want from either of the piles. The player who picks the last pebble wins.
Try this game with your friends. Now, how do you play so that you win?
To find a winning strategy, try playing with 1 pebble in each pile, two in each, three in each, and so on.

content.text:
1. Predict first: with two piles of 1 pebble each, does the first player or the second player win?
2. With 1 and 1: the first player takes one pile, the second takes the last pebble and wins.
3. With 2 and 2, 3 and 3, and so on, the second player wins by copying: whatever the first player takes from one pile, take the same amount from the other pile.
4. Equal piles always stay equal after the second player's move, and the second player takes the last pebble.

content.text:
Worked example: Two piles have 7 pebbles each. You play second. The first player takes 3 from the first pile. What do you do, and who wins?
1. Mirror the move: take 3 from the other pile. Now the piles are 4 and 4.
2. If the first player takes 4 from a pile, take 4 from the other: 0 and 0 and you win.
3. Equal piles after your move, every time, so you take the last pebble.
Answer: Take the same number from the other pile; the second player wins

concepts.concept_name: Mira's puzzle that always ends in 9

content.text:
Now, it's Mira's turn. She gives a fun puzzle to Sanju with the following steps: (a) Take any two different digits. For example 3 and 7. (b) Make two 2-digit numbers using them: 37 and 73. (c) Subtract the smaller number from the bigger number: 73 − 37 = 36.
Now, use the two digits in the difference and repeat steps (b) and (c). Continue this process until you get a 1-digit number. Even before everyone could finish, Mira exclaimed, "Mind you! No matter which two numbers you choose, you will get 9 in the end."
How did Mira know what the 1-digit number in the end would be? Let us explore.

Now, use the two digits in the difference and repeat steps (b) and (c). Continue this process until you get a 1-digit number. Even before everyone could finish, Mira exclaimed, "Mind you! No matter which two numbers you choose, you will get 9 in the end."

content.text:
1. Predict first: take 3 and 7. What do you think you will get at the end?
2. 73 − 37 = 36. Use 3 and 6: 63 − 36 = 27. Use 2 and 7: 72 − 27 = 45. Use 4 and 5: 54 − 45 = 9.
3. Look at the differences: 36, 27, 45, 9. All are in the table of 9.
4. The reason: the difference of the numbers is 9 times the difference of the digits. For 3 and 7, the digits differ by 4, and 36 is 9 times 4.

content.text:
Worked example: Follow Mira's steps for the digits 3 and 7 and say why each difference is a multiple of 9.
1. 73 − 37 = 36, and 36 = 9 × 4, where 7 − 3 = 4.
2. 63 − 36 = 27, and 27 = 9 × 3, where 6 − 3 = 3.
3. 72 − 27 = 45, and 45 = 9 × 5, where 7 − 2 = 5.
4. 54 − 45 = 9, and 9 = 9 × 1, where 5 − 4 = 1.
Answer: 73 − 37 = 36, 63 − 36 = 27, 72 − 27 = 45 and 54 − 45 = 9; every difference is 9 times the difference of the digits

content.text:
Mira's puzzle, explore (1) to (4): Observe the differences in each step. Try the puzzle using another pair of digits. What digits give a 1-digit number in the first step itself? Find different digits such that the difference between the numbers is 27.
1. (1) 36, 27, 45 and 9 are all in the table of 9.
2. (2) Digits 2 and 8: 82 − 28 = 54, then 54 − 45 = 9. The differences are multiples of 9 and the end is 9.
3. (3) Digits that are next to each other, like 4 and 5: 54 − 45 = 9. Their difference is 1.
4. (4) 27 = 9 × 3, so the digits must differ by 3: 1 and 4, 2 and 5, 3 and 6, 4 and 7, 5 and 8, 6 and 9, 0 and 3.
Answer: (1) all in the table of 9 (2) ends in 9 (3) digits that differ by 1, such as 4 and 5 (4) digits that differ by 3, such as 2 and 5

content.text:
Mira's puzzle, the three questions: What do the differences between the digits indicate? List the numbers that give a 1-digit number in the third subtraction. Identify pairs of digits that lead to the 1-digit number after the maximum possible number of subtractions.
1. The difference of the numbers is 9 times the difference of the digits.
2. Third subtraction gives 9: after the second step the difference must be 9 times 1, from digits that differ by 1, like 45, 56, 67 and 78.
3. The longest run: 3 and 7 (36, 27, 45, 9), the run in the book, takes four subtractions.
Answer: The number difference is 9 times the digit difference; the longest runs, like 3 and 7, take four subtractions

tool_config.title: Digit Difference Machine: Why Always 9?
tool_config.idea: Take two different digits, make the two two-digit numbers, subtract the smaller from the bigger and repeat. The difference of the numbers is 9 times the difference of the digits, so every step gives a multiple of 9 and the machine always ends at 9.
tool_config.screen: A machine with two digit slots, an automatic maker of the two numbers, a subtraction panel that shows the bigger and smaller number, a next-step feed that reuses the two digits of the answer, and a table that records digits, digit difference and number difference for each run.
student_does: Choose two different digits in the slots.
Press Make numbers and read the two numbers formed.
Press Subtract and look at the difference.
Repeat with the two digits of the answer until one digit is left, then add the run to the table.
challenges: Run the machine on 3 and 7 and follow it to the end.
Run it on 1 and 9, then on 2 and 8.
Run it on 4 and 5. What do you notice about the first step?
Find two digits whose difference of numbers is 27.
Extend the table: choose digits whose digit difference is 2, 3, 5 and 7.
Find the digits that give the longest run before reaching a one-digit answer.
feedback: Each difference is shown with its digit sum or digit gap, and the multiples of 9 glow in the table.
A run that ends in one digit stamps the digit and adds a row to the table.
A pair of equal digits is turned back with a note that the digits must be different.
tool_config.done_when: Every card is done and at least five rows are in the table.

hint_ladder.text: What do you notice about the differences in the table so far?
Look at the digit difference and the number difference side by side.
Compare the number difference with the digit difference: how many times bigger is it?
For 7 and 3: the digits differ by 4, and 73 minus 37 is 36, which is 9 times 4.

tool_config.design_brief: Class 5 tool brief: interactive and doer-based, the student performs actions and does not only watch. The student can build and rearrange numbers, compare values, place markers on number lines, complete patterns and solve problems. Colourful, clear and engaging: number cards, place value tokens, number lines, arrows, visual counters and real-life travel illustrations, all of which can be selected, moved, changed or arranged. A simple uncluttered layout with one prominent main visual and only the controls that are needed. Immediate visual feedback: numbers update, markers move and correct arrangements are highlighted. Hints and feedback help the student discover the answer and never reveal it. Hands-on, visually engaging and conceptually clear.

maths_rules: each answer is 9 times the gap between its two digits; chain for 3 and 7: 36 (gap 4), 27 (gap 3), 45 (gap 5), 9 (gap 1), four subtractions
the third subtraction gives 9 when the second answer is 45, whose digits 4 and 5 are 1 apart
45 comes from 27 or 72, whose digits are 5 apart; 27 = 9 × 3 and 72 = 9 × 8
so the starting digits are 3 apart (1 and 4, 2 and 5, 3 and 6, 4 and 7, 5 and 8, 6 and 9) or 8 apart (1 and 9)
1 and 9: 91 − 19 = 72, 72 − 27 = 45, 54 − 45 = 9, three subtractions (gap 8)
1 and 3: 31 − 13 = 18, 81 − 18 = 63, 63 − 36 = 27, 72 − 27 = 45, 54 − 45 = 9, five subtractions (gap 2); no other gap gives more than four
slip: a bigger gap does not give more subtractions; 8 apart gives 3, 4 apart gives 4, 2 apart gives 5

open_questions: The worklist answer says the longest runs, like 3 and 7, take four subtractions. Running every pair of digits shows 3 and 7 take four, but digits that are 2 apart (for example 1 and 3: 31 − 13 = 18, 81 − 18 = 63, 63 − 36 = 27, 72 − 27 = 45, 54 − 45 = 9) take five, which is the most. The worklist step also lists 45, 56, 67 and 78 for the third subtraction; running the chains shows a one digit answer at the third subtraction for digits 3 apart or 8 apart. The script teaches the computed result; please confirm which one the book intends.

concepts.concept_name: The caretaker's counting mistake

content.text:
Once upon a time, there was a king who was very fond of horses. He had 20 horses of the best breed. The horses were kept in the royal stable, and cared for by a caretaker.
One night, a thief stole one of the horses. Fearing punishment, the caretaker arranged the horses in the stable as shown in the picture here.
The king counted 5 horses along each side. "We have 5 horses along each side and there are 4 sides. So there are a total of 20 horses, your majesty," the caretaker explained.
But wait, were there really 20 horses in the stable? Count the horses one by one and check! What was the mistake in the caretaker's explanation?

content.text:
1. Predict first: 5 horses on each of 4 sides, so is it always 20 horses?
2. A horse at a corner stands on two sides, so it is counted once for each side.
3. In the caretaker's stable, one corner horse is counted twice. 20 counted − 1 counted twice = 19 horses.
4. The caretaker added 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 without noticing that a corner horse was in two of the fives.

content.text:
Worked example: The caretaker says 5 horses on each of 4 sides makes 20. One horse stands at a corner and is counted on two sides. How many horses are really there?
1. 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 20 counts every corner horse twice.
2. One corner horse is counted twice, so subtract 1: 20 − 1 = 19.
3. There are only 19 horses.
Answer: 19 horses, because the corner horse was counted twice

concepts.concept_name: Eighteen horses and how many more can go

content.text:
The following night, the thief stole another horse from the stable. Now, only 18 horses remained. The caretaker once again cleverly arranged the 18 horses, so that there were 5 horses on each side of the square stable. How do you think he was able to do it? Arrange the 18 horses in the stable with 5 on each side.
How many more horses can the thief steal before the king notices something is wrong? Try making the arrangements yourself.

content.text:
1. Predict first: if 19 horses had 1 corner horse, how many corner horses will 18 horses need?
2. Counted total is 20. Real horses = 20 − (number of corner horses). For 18 horses, 20 − 18 = 2 corner horses.
3. Put horses on 2 corners, and fill the sides so that each side still counts 5.
4. There are 4 corners, so the most corner horses is 4 and the fewest horses is 20 − 4 = 16. The thief can steal 18 − 16 = 2 more horses from 18.

content.text:
Worked example: There are 18 horses. How many corner horses are needed so that each side shows 5, and how many more horses can the thief steal?
1. The count of 20 minus the corner horses is the real number: 20 − 18 = 2 corner horses.
2. All 4 corners hold horses at most, so the fewest horses is 20 − 4 = 16.
3. From 18, the thief can steal 18 − 16 = 2 more horses.
Answer: 2 corner horses are needed, and the thief can steal 2 more horses

content.text:
King's Horses, how many more can be stolen: How many more horses can the thief steal before the king notices something is wrong? Try making the arrangements yourself.
1. 19 horses: 1 corner horse. 18 horses: 2 corner horses. 17 horses: 3 corner horses. 16 horses: 4 corner horses.
2. With 15 horses, 20 − 15 = 5 corner horses would be needed, but there are only 4 corners.
3. So 5 on every side is possible down to 16 horses. The thief can steal 2 more from 18.
Answer: 2 more horses, down to 16; with 15 the king would find 5 on a side is no longer possible

tool_config.title: Square Stable: Five on Every Side
tool_config.idea: In a square ring of horses, a horse at a corner is counted on two sides. With 5 horses counted on each side, 20 counted means fewer real horses when corners hold horses.
tool_config.screen: A square stable drawn as a ring of 24 spots (4 corners and 5 spots between the corners on every side) with a tray of horse tokens, side counters for the four sides, and a total counter that counts every horse once.
student_does: Drag horse tokens to spots on the ring.
Read the four side counters and the total.
Move horses to corners or to side spots and watch the counters change.
Press Check to see whether every side shows 5.
challenges: Place 19 horses so that every side shows 5.
Count the horses one by one and find the caretaker's mistake.
Place 18 horses so that every side shows 5.
Try 17 horses with 5 on every side.
Try 16 horses with 5 on every side.
Try 15 horses with 5 on every side. What happens?
feedback: A horse on a corner lights both its sides, and each side counter goes up by one.

tool_config.design_brief: Class 5 tool brief: interactive and doer-based, the student performs actions and does not only watch. The student can build and rearrange numbers, compare values, place markers on number lines, complete patterns and solve problems. Colourful, clear and engaging: number cards, place value tokens, number lines, arrows, visual counters and real-life travel illustrations, all of which can be selected, moved, changed or arranged. A simple uncluttered layout with one prominent main visual and only the controls that are needed. Immediate visual feedback: numbers update, markers move and correct arrangements are highlighted. Hints and feedback help the student discover the answer and never reveal it. Hands-on, visually engaging and conceptually clear.

concepts.concept_name: What we learned in We the Travellers - I

content.text:
1. Ten thousand is 10 thousands, written 10,000, in a new TTh column.
2. Five-digit numbers are read from the thousands part and written with commas and number names.
3. To compare numbers, count the digits first; with equal digits, compare from the left.
4. The nearest ten, hundred or thousand is the neighbour with the fewest jumps.
5. Distance in many hours is the distance in one hour times the hours, and vehicles needed come from dividing people by seats.
6. Puzzles teach us to think strategically: the pile of pebbles is won by mirroring, and a corner horse is counted twice.

video_script.why: The child has met all the ideas of the chapter and now needs them together on one board before moving on.
video_script.substitution: Say each idea in one line, then ask one rounding question with new numbers.
video_script.anchor: a numbered board of the six ideas of the chapter, drawn like a train route with six stops

final_answer.spoken: six thousand three hundred

maths_rules: 10 thousands = 10,000, which needs a new TTh column
5-digit numbers are read from the thousands part, with commas and number names
compare: count the digits first; with equal digits compare from the left
round to the nearest ten, hundred or thousand: pick the neighbour with the fewest jumps
distance = distance in one hour x number of hours; vehicles needed = people divided by seats
pebble game: take the same number from the other pile (mirroring); a corner horse is counted on two sides, so take away 1
your turn: 6,284 lies between 6,200 and 6,300; 84 is more than 50, so it is nearer 6,300; answer 6,300; never shown
video_script.design: Six numbered lines on a train route board, one idea each, then one rounding question with new numbers. Nothing new is taught.

beats.on_screen: a train route board appears; stop 1 reads ten thousand is 10 thousands, a new column; stop 2 reads read 5-digit numbers from the thousands part, with commas and names

marks.one: stop 1 reads ten thousand is 10 thousands, a new column
marks.left: the new column glows to the left of the thousands
marks.two: stop 2 reads read 5-digit numbers from the thousands part, with commas and names

narration: <bookmark mark='one'/>Idea one is that ten thousand is ten thousands, and it needs a new column.
<bookmark mark='left'/>That column sits to the left of the thousands.
<bookmark mark='two'/>Idea two is that five digit numbers are read from the thousands part first. We then write them with commas and number names.

beats.on_screen: stop 3 reads count the digits first, then compare from the left; stop 4 reads round to the nearest ten, hundred or thousand; the fewest jumps is circled

marks.three: stop 3 reads count the digits first, then compare from the left
marks.left: an arrow runs from the left digit across the number
marks.four: stop 4 reads round to the nearest ten, hundred or thousand

narration: <bookmark mark='three'/>Idea three is to compare numbers by counting the digits first. With equal digits, compare from the left.
<bookmark mark='left'/>Compare each place from the left, and stop at the first place that differs.
<bookmark mark='four'/>Idea four is rounding to the nearest ten, hundred or thousand.
<bookmark mark='jumps'/>Pick the neighbour that needs the fewest jumps.

beats.on_screen: stop 5 reads distance in one hour times the hours; vehicles needed come from people divided by seats; stop 6 reads puzzles need a plan; mirror the move; a corner horse is counted on two sides

marks.five: stop 5 reads distance in one hour times the hours
marks.cars: the line vehicles needed come from people divided by seats appears
marks.six: stop 6 reads puzzles need a plan
marks.mirror: the words mirror the move appear beside two equal piles
marks.corner: the words a corner horse is counted on two sides appear beside the stable

narration: <bookmark mark='five'/>Idea five is that distance in many hours is the distance in one hour times the hours.
<bookmark mark='cars'/>Vehicles needed come from dividing the people by the seats.
<bookmark mark='six'/>Idea six is that puzzles teach us to think with a plan.
<bookmark mark='mirror'/>In the pebble game, mirroring means taking the same number from the other pile.
<bookmark mark='corner'/>A corner horse is counted on two sides, so we take away one.

beats.on_screen: the board shrinks to the side; a number line shows 6,284 with two empty boxes, one hundred before it and one hundred after it; an empty box appears beside the words nearest hundred

marks.turn: a number line shows 6,284 with two empty boxes, one hundred before it and one hundred after it
marks.ask: an empty box appears beside the words nearest hundred

narration: <bookmark mark='turn'/>Your turn. Look at the number six thousand two hundred eighty four on the line.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Which hundred is it nearest to?

objectives.objective_text: Students count in thousands up to 9,000 and say that adding one more thousand gives ten thousand.
Students extend the place value chart with a TTh column, state that 10 thousands is 1 ten thousand and that 10 tens, 10 hundreds and 10 thousands each make the next place, and write 10,000.
Students read and write a number as thousands, hundreds, tens and ones, such as 1,380 and 9,123, using the same ten digits in different places.
Students build numbers from ones to ten thousand by dropping tokens in the place value chart, watch ten tokens regroup into one of the next place, and read each number aloud.
Students write the numbers made by 10,000 and a few ones or tens, such as 10,001, 10,002, 10,010 and 10,024, in the chart and in words.
Students count the tokens of each kind to write a number such as 10,033, 10,458, 11,214 or 13,520, fill its TTh, Th, H, T, O digits and say its name.
Students write 13,520, 20,000 and 45,867 as numbers and in words and see that the thousands part is read first.
Students build five-digit numbers from tokens, write each number with commas in the TTh to O chart, and write the number name from the thousands part first.
Attempt each practice question independently, working through every step before viewing the video solution and checking the answer.

Attempt each practice question independently, working through every step before viewing the video solution and checking the answer.
